The Dash-and-dot goatfish Parupeneus barberinus is a common mullid species inhabiting sandy and seagrass habitats across the Indo-Pacific region. Females produce between 70 and 80 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = between 70 and 80 eggs per spawning event], with individuals typically participating in multiple spawning events over the course of a breeding season at a rate of approximately one spawning event every two weeks [F_R_i = approximately one spawning event every two weeks] when water temperatures reach 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C]. The fertilised ovum, a small pelagic egg measuring about 1 mm in diameter, gives rise to a yolk-sac larva following eclosion. At the moment of hatching, the newly emerged prolarva carries an endogenous yolk reserve that supports its initial development; the wet weight at birth is estimated at 0.00062 grams [Wwb = 0.00062 grams], reflecting the modest provisioning invested per offspring in this planktonic spawning strategy.

Growth proceeds rapidly during the early juvenile phase as the fish shifts to exogenous feeding and begins exploiting benthic invertebrate prey. The ultimate fork length attained by adults in this population reaches 28 centimeters [Li = 28 centimeters], a size that is consistent with values reported for congeneric species occupying similar trophic niches in the tropical Indo-West Pacific. This asymptotic length is typically achieved after several years of sustained somatic growth under favourable resource conditions. Juveniles recruit to seagrass beds and adjacent sand flats where they forage on small crustaceans and polychaetes, and the progressive accumulation of body mass underpins the transition to the reproductively mature stage. Field records indicate that the wet weight at puberty, associated with the onset of gonad maturation, is approximately 285.5 grams [Wwi = approximately 285.5 grams], a body size that signals the investment of resources directed toward gamete production and spawning activity.

The fork length at which individuals typically attain sexual maturity, marking the pubertal transition, is 13 centimeters [Lp = 13 centimeters]. This measurement was derived from extensive field surveys examining gonadal development across multiple size classes, and it represents the length at which half of the sampled individuals showed evidence of active gametogenesis or prior spawning histories. The ultimate wet weight reached by adults is estimated to be 26.5 grams [Wwp = 26.5 grams], based on length-weight relationships established from local specimens. This mass threshold underscores the considerable size range over which this species matures, as the difference between the mass at puberty and the ultimate adult mass reflects the continued somatic investment that occurs even after reproductive capability is first achieved. The protracted growth trajectory likely enhances fecundity at larger body sizes, a pattern commonly observed among iteroparous teleosts that spawn repeatedly across multiple seasons.

Longevity records for Parupeneus barberinus from a mark-recapture study conducted in the warm tropical waters of the Great Barrier Reef indicate that the oldest documented individual survived for 5 years [am = 5 years], with the study site characterised by an average water temperature of 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C]. This lifespan aligns reasonably well with estimates for other tropical mullids of comparable adult body size, although a degree of intraspecific variation is likely across the species' broad geographic range. The achievement of this maximum age is presumably constrained by predation pressure from larger piscivores, as well as by the metabolic costs associated with maintaining a consistently high activity level in warm-water environments. The data from this particular study were gathered over a decade-long sampling program, ensuring that the longevity estimate is robust and representative of the natural mortality schedule experienced by the population.

Reproductive output peaks when females attain their largest body sizes, with the maximum daily reproduction rate reaching an average of approximately 72 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 72 eggs per day] under the prevailing thermal regime of 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C]. This elevated fecundity is sustained through repeated spawning events during the extended breeding season, which spans several months in tropical latitudes. The capability for such high daily egg production reflects the substantial energetic reserves that can be accumulated by large, reproductively active females that have completed their primary somatic growth phase. Comparative data from related mullid species suggest that the reproductive strategy of Parupeneus barberinus is characterised by high fecundity and relatively small egg size, a combination that is well suited to the unpredictable survival prospects of pelagic larvae in coral reef ecosystems. Management of local fisheries often takes this reproductive capacity into account when setting sustainable harvest limits.
